deep.reconstruction:
Setting (Gauss's own words, paraphrased): a, b, c, d are four points on the unit circle, identified with complex numbers. A prime (') denotes the complex conjugate ('Adjunkte'). On the unit circle a' = 1/a, etc.

Definitions:
- p = intersection of chords ab and cd.
- q = intersection of chords ac and bd.
- r = intersection of chords ad and bc.
- p*, q*, r* are the midpoints of the chords whose end-tangents meet at p, q, r. In modern terms p* is the inverse of p in the unit circle, i.e. the foot of the polar of p on the ray Op.

(1) Intersection of two chords. Standard (my gloss): the intersection of chords xy and zw on the unit circle is (xy(z+w) - zw(x+y))/(xy - zw). Gauss writes:
- p = (abc+abd-acd-bcd)/(ab-cd) = a - b(a-c)(a-d)/(ab-cd)
- q = (abc+acd-abd-bcd)/(ac-bd) = a - c(a-b)(a-d)/(ac-bd)
- r = (acd+abd-abc-bcd)/(ad-bc) = a - d(a-b)(a-c)/(ad-bc)
The 'a - ...' forms follow by expanding a(ab-cd) - b(a-c)(a-d), etc.

(2) Difference p - q. Subtracting the 'a - ...' forms and factoring gives
p - q = (a-d)(b-c)(abd+acd-abc-bcd)/((ab-cd)(ac-bd)).
The last numerator equals r(ad-bc), so
p - q = (a-d)(b-c)(ad-bc) r / ((ab-cd)(ac-bd)).

(3) The point p*. Using a' = 1/a, one gets p' = (a+b-c-d)/(ab-cd). Hence
p* = 1/p' = (ab-cd)/(a+b-c-d) = a - (a-c)(a-d)/(a+b-c-d).

(4) Difference p* - q:
p* - q = (a-d)(b-c)(ad-bc)/((ac-bd)(a+b-c-d)).
Multiplying and dividing by (ab-cd), this is p* · (a-d)(b-c)(ad-bc)/((ab-cd)(ac-bd)). By (2) that equals p*(p-q)/r.
So r(p* - q) = p*(p - q), i.e. p*(q + r - p) = qr. By symmetry:
- q*(p + r - q) = pr
- r*(p + q - r) = pq

Purpose (completed on the next page, f.213): the ratios (r-q)/(p*-q) etc. are shown to be real. Hence p*, q, r are collinear and the line is normal to O p* p. In other words, the line qr is the polar of p. So the diagonal triangle pqr of a cyclic quadrangle is self-polar with respect to the circle, and the centre O is its orthocenter (Brocard's theorem). The method is pure complex-number coordinates with conjugation on the unit circle.

The red-pencil note '[Mittheil. =0' appears to be a later archivist/editor annotation, not part of the mathematics.
errors: No mathematical errors found; all identities check out symbolically.
The ink blots in the lines for p and p* stand where minus signs belong ('= a - ...'); these are not errors in content.

results.what: Complex-coordinate formula for the intersection of two chords of the unit circle: p = (ab(c+d) - cd(a+b))/(ab-cd)
results.modern_name: Chord-intersection formula in unit-circle complex coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore of complex-number geometry (systematized in 19th–20th c. texts, e.g. Morley, Deaux)

results.modern_name: Inversion in the unit circle / pole–polar in complex coordinates

results.what: p*(q+r-p) = qr (and cyclic): p* lies on line qr, so qr is the polar of p, and O p ⟂ qr
results.modern_name: Self-polar diagonal triangle of an inscribed quadrangle; Brocard's theorem (circumcentre is orthocentre of the diagonal triangle)
results.usually_credited_to: Pole–polar property: La Hire (1685)/Desargues, Poncelet (1822); orthocentre form: H. Brocard (late 19th c.)

deep.surprise_reason: The geometric content (polar of a diagonal point passes through the other two) was classical projective geometry by Gauss's time. Gauss's elegant proof by complex coordinates on the unit circle, and the compact relation p*(q+r-p)=qr, is a nice unpublished early instance of complex-number geometry. It anticipates the orthocentre formulation later known as Brocard's theorem. Notable but not a major new result.

checkable.asserts: p is the standard chord-intersection formula

transcription_corrections: In p and p*, the blot after '= a' is a minus sign: 'a - b(a-c)(a-d)/(ab-cd)' and 'a - (a-c)(a-d)/(a+b-c-d)'.
In the q numerator, 'abC+acd' (the C is overwritten) reads abc+acd; the transcription is correct.
Cancelled text after p* is 'q*, r*' (struck through); the transcription is correct.
